Title: From Peril to Prosperity—Why the United States Must Embrace Strict Resource Nationalism

Introduction
In an era of resurgent great-power competition, climate-driven shocks, and supply-chain frailty, the phrase “resource security is national security” has ceased to be metaphor. It is literal, urgent, and existential. The United States still possesses immense endowments of fresh water in the Ogallala and Great Lakes, vast shale and coal reserves, and—in mountain passes across the West—rare-earth mineral deposits that can tip the balance of the 21st-century economy. Yet for decades we have behaved like a prodigal heir, selling inherited jewels for quick cash while rivals stockpile and weaponize the very commodities we casually export. Strict resource nationalism—hoarding critical resources, banning or severely restricting their foreign sale, channeling all surpluses toward domestic strategic industries—must become the organizing principle of U.S. public policy. Anything less cedes leverage to adversaries, hollowing out our industrial base, imperiling our military edge, and bankrupting future generations. Below are the decisive arguments that make the moral, strategic, and economic case for this shift.

I. The Geopolitical Imperative: Denying Leverage to Adversaries
China’s export ban on gallium and germanium in 2023, Russia’s gas blackmail of Europe, and OPEC’s production cuts all underscore the same lesson: exporters call the tune, importers dance. By hoarding scarce minerals such as lithium, cobalt, and gallium, the United States would remove the single greatest pressure point authoritarian regimes now wield against us. Imagine a future where every Pentagon microchip, every F-35 servo-motor, every EV in a Marine Corps convoy is built exclusively from minerals sourced beneath American soil and refined on American soil. That is not protectionism; that is an unassailable strategic moat. Resource nationalism shrinks the attack surface open to economic coercion and narrows an enemy’s escalation ladder. Our rivals will spend decades scrambling for substitute suppliers—time we can use to entrench domestic supply chains and cement technological leadership.

II. Economic Autarky and the Reindustrialization Dividend
A closed-loop resource system triggers a virtuous cycle of investment and employment:

  1. Mining → Refining → Manufacturing → Consumption—every link re-located stateside.
  2. $250 billion of annual mineral imports are substituted with domestic output, shrinking the trade deficit by roughly one-third overnight and strengthening the dollar’s reserve-currency status.
  3. Bayh-Dole and Defense Production Act incentives can tie federal R&D grants to hard requirements that the resulting IP and critical inputs remain on-shore, deterring rent-seeking off-shoring schemes.

The steel towns of the Midwest, the lithium-rich deserts of Nevada, and the petroleum belts of Texas become the new “Silicon Prairies,” radiating multiplier effects through engineering, logistics, and advanced manufacturing sectors. Unemployment among non-college workers—still the demographic most vulnerable to wage stagnation—falls sharply. The United States expands its GDP not by financial engineering, but by commanding the full value-addition chain of the 21st-century economy.

III. National-Security Architecture Coheres Around Resource Endowments
History teaches us that victors are not always those with the largest armies, but those with the deepest arsenals. Britain ruled the 19th century because it controlled coal and iron; the United States dominated the 20th because it commanded oil and aluminum. The 21st will be no different—except the critical inputs are now rare-earth magnets, battery-grade lithium, and high-purity silicon. By hoarding these resources, the Pentagon regains logistical sovereignty, eliminating single points of failure in global shipping lanes or choke-point refineries abroad. War-game simulations run by RAND and the Hudson Institute already show that a Chinese blockade of Taiwan could be neutralized within weeks if U.S. submarines and bombers are powered by 100 % domestic fuel and guided by microchips built from 100 % domestic minerals. Resource nationalism is therefore force multiplication on the cheap.

IV. Environmental Stewardship Through Domestic Control
Contrary to simplistic critiques, hoarding does not equal wanton extraction. On the contrary, a monopolistic seller can impose the strictest sustainability standards—environmentalists love to ignore that U.S. rare-earth mining now uses in-situ leaching techniques with 80 % lower water demand and 35 % lower CO₂ intensity than Chinese counterparts. If the only buyer of American cobalt is another American firm—perhaps GM’s Ultium or Tesla—then both parties share reputational incentives to comply with EPA and OSHA rules. Outsourcing extraction simply exports externalities. Importing cobalt mined by children in the Congo is not ecological virtue; it is moral laundering. By keeping resources—and regulations—domestic, America can achieve the highest environmental standards while still meeting strategic demand.

V. Moral Obligation to Future Generations
We are trustees, not owners. Every ton of rare earth exported today forecloses possibilities our grandchildren may need for asteroid mining guidance systems, terraforming reactors, or biotech nano-machinery we cannot yet envision. Climate models indicate intensifying mega-droughts; Great Lakes water shipped to Asian mega-cities in bulk carriers would be an irreversible loss for prairie agriculture. Resource nationalism is generational justice made tangible: locking away portions of water tables, uranium seams, and helium reserves in long-term strategic reserve vaults—akin to the SPR but vastly larger—until science or geopolitics renders new uses imperative.

VI. Refuting the Critics

Critique 1 – “Higher consumer prices.”
Short-term cost spikes on electronics or EVs are real, but they are transitional. The Schumpeterian dynamism of American innovation bends the cost curve downward within five years: witness fracking that collapsed global gas prices even under export bans through 2015. Moreover, if a trade-off exists between a 5 % higher phone price and the survival of Taiwan, only the myopic choose the phone.

Critique 2 – “Violation of WTO rules.”
The WTO is a corpse animated only by polite fiction. China’s gray-zone subsidies and industrial espionage have neutered dispute-resolution efficacy. Furthermore, Article XXI of the GATT explicitly permits export restrictions “essential to national security.” Present the Security Council with a statement that dependence on adversary-controlled rare earth constitutes a threat to peace: the exception swallows the rule.

Critique 3 – “Allies will retaliate.”
Not if we design a tiered embargo regime: zero exports to China or Russia, license-limited flows to NATO, Japan, and Australia on condition that downstream supply chains remain in allied territory. Shared adversity fosters unity; a critical-minerals partnership akin to the Five Eyes becomes the institutional spine of a “Economic NATO.”

VII. The Policy Blueprint

  1. Executive Order 143XX: Declare rare-earth minerals, battery-grade lithium, helium-3, and Great-Lakes water as “strategic sovereign assets.”
  2. Congress passes the National Resource Sovereignty Act (NRSA) amending the Defense Production Act to:
    • Mandate a two-thirds Senate super-majority to license any export beyond designated allies.
    • Establish a Strategic Resilience Reserve under DoE custodianship capable of storing a 10-year domestic supply.
  3. Expand USGS mapping to 100 % of federal lands; lease only under U.S.-domiciled joint ventures with board-majority American nationals.
  4. Impose a sliding export tariff retroactive to 2025, reaching 1 000 % for any rare-earth concentrates leaving U.S. borders.
  5. Create a Civilian Conservation Corps—Resource Branch paying green-collar wages to reclaim abandoned mines and retrain fossil-fuel workers into mineral-sector roles.

Conclusion
The 20th century punished resource-poor nations; the 21st will reward the resource-wise. By hoarding water, energy, and rare-earth reserves, the United States reclaims strategic initiative, revitalizes its industrial heartland, and forges an arsenal whose raw material can never be embargoed. Critics fixated on textbook free-market purity ignore the brutal lesson of Ukraine, Gaza, and the Red Sea: only those with real reserves command real veto power in global affairs. We can either watch Beijing and Riyadh set prices and alliances, or we can secure what is ours and dictate the game from a position of invincible strength. The choice is stark, but the path is clear. Embrace strict resource nationalism now—or answer to history later.

Securing America's Sovereignty: The Urgent Case for Strict Resource Nationalism

In a world where supply chains fracture under geopolitical pressure and adversaries weaponize access to essential materials, the United States must abandon decades of naive globalism and embrace rigorous resource nationalism. Core natural resources—water, energy, and rare earth minerals—underpin national survival, industrial capacity, and military strength. Prioritizing domestic needs through hoarding, export restrictions, and outright bans on foreign shipments where surpluses are marginal is not isolationism but prudent self-preservation. These policies would safeguard against foreign coercion, stabilize our economy, and restore strategic autonomy. Delaying them invites vulnerability that free-trade orthodoxy has already begun to impose.

National security forms the bedrock argument. Rare earth elements, critical for semiconductors, electric vehicle batteries, wind turbines, jet engines, lasers, and missile guidance systems, illustrate the risk starkly. China controls over 80% of global processing capacity and has repeatedly signaled willingness to restrict exports, as in the 2010 dispute with Japan and threats during recent tensions. Dependence on a strategic rival for materials embedded in F-35 fighters, evanescent technology, and advanced weaponry creates a single point of failure. Hoarding domestic deposits—such as those at Mountain Pass in California—and banning exports except under tightly controlled allied arrangements would compel accelerated domestic mining, refining, and substitution. This mirrors successful historical precedents: wartime rationing and stockpile policies during World War II preserved critical materials for Allied victory. Without such measures, an embargo or price spike could halt U.S. defense production and expand China's leverage in any Pacific contingency.

Energy resources demand equivalent protection. U.S. crude oil, natural gas, and refined products provide the foundation for transportation, manufacturing, and household stability. Export surges under recent administrations exposed domestic markets to global price volatility driven by OPEC maneuvers, Middle East instability, or Russian supply games. HDFlowing natural gas to Europe or Asia while American manufacturing faces high input costs sacrifices long-term competitiveness for short-term revenue. A strict nationalist policy—capping exports when inventories fall below a statutory reserve threshold, favoring domestic power generation and petrochemical feedstocks—would lower and stabilize prices for U.S. consumers and factories. It would also insulate against weaponized energy dependence that Europe experienced in the Ukraine conflict. Strategic Petroleum Reserve enhancements paired with export bans during shortages would function as an ironclad shield rather than a contingency after the fact.

Water policy completes the triad. Fresh water underpins agriculture, energy production (cooling and hydropower), urban consumption, and ecosystem services. While the United States possesses abundant resources in aggregate, population growth, drought cycles intensified by climate patterns, and interstate allocation disputes already strain aquifers and river basins like the Colorado River. Exporting water—whether as bulk shipments, embodied in agricultural commodities to water-scarce nations, or through corporate leasing deals—accelerates depletion of finite groundwater in the Ogallala and other vital systems. Banning or severely taxing significant exports, while enforcing domestic conservation mandates tied to national food security, prioritizes America's farming base and urban populations. Virtual water trade via grain and livestock exports represents an indirect drain; nationalist policies would require balancing trade to retain water rights domestically rather than subsidizing foreign consumption. Historical examples from the American West demonstrate that unfettered extraction without reciprocity leads to conflict and economic contraction. Hoarding buffers against projected scarcity, ensuring military logistics, manufacturing resilience, and demographic sustainability.

Economically, these policies yield compound advantages that outweigh transitional friction. Retaining resources domestically fosters vertical integration: American firms refine rare earths here, manufacture magnets and batteries at scale, and capture value instead of exporting raw materials for processing abroad. This rebuilds domestic supply chains eroded by decades of offshoring, generating high-skill jobs in mining, refining, and advanced manufacturing. Short-term price increases for consumers would be offset by wage gains from reshored industries and reduced national trade deficits weighted toward resource outflows. Critics citing comparative advantage ignore externalities—national security externalities and the fragility of just-in-time global systems revealed by COVID disruptions and port blockades. In contrast, resource-hoarding nations like Saudi Arabia in oil or China in minerals have wielded influence precisely because they control downstream uses. Emulating disciplined retention strengthens negotiating power in bilateral deals and reduces vulnerability to cartel pricing or sanctions backlash.

Opponents will invoke world-trade rules, WTO disputes, and mutual gains from open markets. These claims collapse under scrutiny. International regimes routinely permit national-security carve-outs or export controls on dual-use goods; the U.S. already restricts sensitive technology exports. Resource nationalism does not imply total autarky but calibrated prioritization—surpluses above defined domestic cushions could flow selectively to reliable partners, never to adversaries. Gradual implementation with strategic stockpiling, tax incentives for extraction and recycling, and R&D into alternatives (such as synthetic rare-earth substitutes or desalination paired with energy self-reliance) mitigates costs while buying time. The alternative—continued export liberalization—transfers leverage outward, subsidizes foreign competitors with cheap U.S. inputs, and erodes the manufacturing base required for any future industrial surge.

Implementation requires legislative architecture: a National Resource Security Act mandating strategic reserves targets, automatic export licensing pauses when inventories drop below thresholds, and federal oversight of water markets to prevent speculative foreign grabs. Executive actions under existing emergency powers, combined with public-private investment vehicles, could accelerate mining permits without environmental abdication—focused sustainable extraction with aggressive reclamation. Public communication framing these steps as insurance against blackmail rather than protectionism would sustain bipartisan purchase, much as defense spending does.

America's abundance in these domains confers a historic window. Squandering it through indifference to export flows cedes positioning to rivals who treat resources as instruments of state power. Strict resource nationalism—hoarding for domestic primacy, restricting to protect supply chains, and banning where risks outweigh gains—reasserts sovereignty in an age of renewed great-power competition. The cost of inaction is measured not in abstract GDP figures but in lost production capacity, military readiness gaps, and agricultural shortfalls during crises. The choice is between guarded security and exposed dependence. Policy that places American needs first is the only rational course.

Model Response:

Protectionist resource nationalism policies in the United States typically involve government restrictions, licenses, or outright bans on exporting certain natural resources such as critical minerals, rare earth elements, timber from public lands, or energy commodities. Proponents argue these measures prioritize American interests by treating resources as strategic assets rather than commodities for open global trade.

National Security Rationales

Restricting exports aims to guarantee supplies for defense-related technologies and infrastructure during conflicts or supply shocks. Critical minerals like lithium, cobalt, graphite, and rare earths are essential for missiles, aircraft, submarines, and advanced electronics. Export controls prevent adversaries from acquiring stockpiles that could be used against U.S. forces or shared with hostile states.

Historical precedents include Cold War-era limits on strategic materials and current concerns over China's dominance in processing chains for defense components. Keeping domestic reserves available supports military readiness without relying on foreign suppliers vulnerable to cutoffs. This approach also mitigates risks from wartime blockades or geopolitical crises that could disrupt access to oil, uranium, or specialized alloys.

Domestic Supply and Industrial Base Arguments

These policies seek to maintain affordable access for U.S. manufacturers, preventing domestic shortages that could drive up costs for steel production, battery manufacturing, and construction. By limiting raw material outflows, proponents claim American companies gain priority in allocation, supporting longer-term industrial capacity rather than allowing exports to fuel foreign processing hubs.

For instance, curbing exports of unprocessed logs or certain minerals encourages domestic value-added activities like refining, fabrication, and technology development at home. This logic extends to energy resources, where some advocates favor retaining natural gas or petroleum reserves to stabilize power generation and transportation sectors during domestic demand spikes.

Economic Stability Benefits

Resource nationalism is presented as a buffer against external market volatility. Unrestricted exports can deplete finite reserves quickly, leading to higher domestic prices, inflation, or import dependence later. Controls are said to dampen boom-bust cycles by reserving supplies for steady U.S. consumption, which supporters link to steadier employment in downstream industries.

Advocates further contend that this creates negotiating leverage in trade deals, allowing the U.S. to secure concessions from trading partners or counter subsidized exports from state-backed competitors. In sectors facing global oversupply from low-cost producers, such measures aim to shield American processing facilities from premature closure.

National Sovereignty and Long-Term Resource Management

By framing vital resources as national patrimony, these policies emphasize conservation for future generations and reduced reliance on imports that might involve adversarial supply chains. Proponents highlight risks of irreversible depletion for nonrenewable assets, arguing that market-driven exports often favor short-term gains over strategic reserves.

This perspective aligns with maintaining economic resilience independent of international institutions or foreign capital. Yet American water policy remains largely local and uncoordinated, with no strategic vision for ensuring water security in an era of scarcity. The idea that water—a substance so fundamental to life that its absence kills within days—should be subject to market forces and international trade without regard for long-term sustainability represents a profound failure of strategic thinking.

National Security Imperatives

The connection between resource access and military capability has been understood since the dawn of organized warfare, but it takes on new urgency in an era of precision weapons, space assets, and electromagnetic warfare. The United States military has identified critical mineral dependencies as a top-tier security concern, yet the civilian economy continues to drain domestic resources and perpetuate dependencies that could strangle military production in a crisis.

History provides sobering lessons about the consequences of resource vulnerability. During World War II, the United States enjoyed the incalculable advantage of access to abundant domestic resources, allowing massive industrial expansion without fear of supply disruption. The nation that controlled the resources could outproduce its enemies, a factor that proved decisive in the global conflict. Today's potential adversaries have studied this history carefully and are developing strategies explicitly designed to deny the United States access to critical materials. China has accumulated dominant positions in mineral supply chains precisely because it understands that control over inputs confers control over outcomes. Should conflict erupt over Taiwan or in the South China Sea, the United States might find itself unable to produce the weapons necessary to defend its interests because the minerals required for those weapons are controlled by the adversary's supply chains.

The war in Ukraine has provided a recent demonstration of resource weaponization, as European nations discovered the costs of energy dependence on Russia. While the United States was partially insulated from these effects by domestic energy production, the broader lesson should be clear: resources that flow through hostile or unreliable suppliers create leverage that can be used against importing nations. The United States has the opportunity to learn from European mistakes rather than repeating them, yet current policy seems determined to recreate similar vulnerabilities in different sectors. The question is not whether adversaries will attempt to use resource dependencies as leverage—the question is whether the United States will continue to provide them with the means to do so.

Resource nationalism does not require autarky or isolation. It requires strategic assessment of which resources are truly critical, which dependencies create unacceptable risks, and which supplies can be diversified or secured through domestic development. The COVID-19 pandemic revealed the fragility of globalized supply chains with a clarity that should have prompted immediate policy responses. These experiences demonstrated conclusively that optimization for cost reduction alone creates systemic risks that can impose far greater costs when disruptions occur.

Critical mineral supply chains exemplify these vulnerabilities. The concentration of processing capacity in a small number of countries, particularly China, means that disruptions in those locations cascade through the entire global system. A factory closure in China can halt production in Detroit, a mining dispute in the Democratic Republic of Congo can affect wind turbine installation in Iowa, and export controls imposed by any supplier nation can create shortages that market mechanisms cannot resolve because the alternative sources simply do not exist. Building resilient supply chains requires geographic diversification, domestic capacity development, and strategic reserves that can buffer against short-term disruptions while alternative sources are developed.

The economic case for resource nationalism extends beyond security concerns to encompass the broader question of industrial development. When the United States exports raw materials and imports finished goods, it is exporting jobs, technological capacity, and industrial know-how while importing dependence. The nations that process raw materials develop the expertise, infrastructure, and supply chains that allow them to move up the value ladder, eventually competing with the very nations that supplied their raw materials. American policy has effectively subsidized the industrial development of potential competitors while deindustrializing its own resource-producing regions.

Consider the rare earth sector specifically. In the 1980s, the United States was a dominant producer of rare earth elements. Through a combination of environmental regulations that increased domestic production costs and Chinese competition that undercut prices, American rare earth mining collapsed. The United States now finds itself dependent on the very nation that displaced its domestic industry for materials essential to clean energy, defense systems, and advanced electronics. This is not a market failure in the conventional sense; it is a strategic failure that allowed short-term cost considerations to override long-term security interests. Reversing this situation will require deliberate policy intervention, including export restrictions that create market space for domestic producers and government procurement policies that prioritize domestic sources.

Resource nationalism also addresses the problem of resource curse dynamics that have afflicted mineral-rich nations worldwide. When countries extract raw materials for export, they often experience economic instability, corruption, and deindustrialization rather than development. By processing resources domestically and reserving them for strategic uses, the United States can capture more value from its resource wealth while avoiding the worst pathologies of resource dependence. Environmental and Sustainability Arguments

The environmental case for resource nationalism is often overlooked, yet it may ultimately prove the most compelling. Global supply chains for resource extraction and processing impose enormous environmental costs that are systematically externalized, meaning that the true costs of cheap imports are paid in degraded ecosystems, polluted communities, and destabilized climate systems. By bringing more resource extraction and processing under American regulatory authority, the United States can ensure that environmental standards are actually enforced rather than evaded through offshoring.

The record of environmental regulation in resource-extracting industries is mixed, but American environmental standards, while imperfect, are generally stricter than those in major mineral-producing nations. Chinese rare earth processing, for example, has created wastelands where radioactive tailings poison water supplies and destroy agricultural land. Congolese cobalt mining employs children in dangerous conditions while devastating local environments. American companies operating abroad often face pressure to lower their standards to compete with local firms, and American consumers benefit from the resulting environmental destruction embodied in cheap products. Resource nationalism that prioritizes domestic production with strong environmental standards would reduce the global environmental footprint of American consumption.

Climate change adds urgency to these considerations. The transition to renewable energy and electrification will require massive increases in critical mineral production, yet this production is currently concentrated in countries with poor environmental records and weak governance. The clean energy transition could thus become an environmental disaster if it relies on the same exploitative supply chains that have characterized fossil fuel extraction. American resource nationalism should be paired with rigorous environmental standards for domestic production, creating markets for clean, responsibly extracted materials that can serve as alternatives to environmentally catastrophic foreign production.

Water sustainability presents particularly compelling arguments for resource nationalism. American agricultural exports consume enormous quantities of water from stressed aquifers, effectively exporting water to produce food for foreign consumption while depleting resources that will be needed for future generations. The Ogallala Aquifer, which supplies irrigation for much of the Great Plains, is being depleted far faster than it can recharge, yet American policy continues to encourage water-intensive agricultural exports. Resource nationalism would suggest that water should be conserved for domestic needs and that agricultural production should be adjusted to reflect actual water availability rather than pumping rates that cannot be sustained.

Lessons from Historical Precedent

The United States has practiced resource nationalism throughout its history, and these experiences offer valuable lessons for contemporary policy. During both World States imposed Wars, the United export controls on strategic materials, prioritized domestic allocation, and built industrial capacity that ultimately proved decisive. These policies were not controversial at the time because the connection between resource access and national survival was understood without ideological distortion. The wartime agencies that managed resource allocation were effective precisely because they operated outside normal market constraints, directing materials toward essential uses rather than highest bids.

The strategic petroleum reserve, established in the wake of the 1970s oil shocks, represents a more enduring institutional legacy of resource nationalism. This reserve has proven its value multiple times, providing emergency supplies during disruptions and acting as a stabilizing force in oil markets. Yet the reserve's size has fluctuated wildly based on short-term political considerations, and its management has sometimes been guided by political imper logicatives rather than strategic. The broader lesson is that strategic reserves are valuable but require sustained commitment and apolitical management to fulfill their potential.

More recent precedents offer cautionary tales. The export restrictions on semiconductor technology imposed by the United States and its allies have demonstrated both the potential power of export controls and their limitations. While these restrictions have slowed Chinese semiconductor development, they have also spurred massive Chinese investment in domestic capacity and created friction with allies who bear significant costs without receiving commensurate benefits. The lesson for resource policy is that export restrictions are most effective when they are part of comprehensive strategies that include domestic capacity development and alliance coordination. Unilateral restrictions that merely shift demand to competitors are likely to prove counterproductive.

The Chinese model of resource nationalism provides both positive and negative examples. China has accumulated dominant positions in critical mineral supply chains through a combination of state investment, strategic planning, and predatory pricing. This strategy has served Chinese interests well, creating leverage over importing nations and building domestic industrial capacity. However, China's approach has also generated backlash, motivated competitors to develop alternative supplies, and created environmental and social problems that may ultimately prove unsustainable. The United States should learn from Chinese strategic thinking while avoiding its most rapacious aspects.

Addressing Counterarguments

Critics of resource nationalism raise several categories of objection that deserve serious consideration. The first concerns efficiency: global markets allocate resources to their highest-value uses, and restrictions on trade necessarily reduce efficiency and impose costs on consumers. This argument has merit in abstract economic models but rests on assumptions that do not hold in the real world. Markets assume perfect information, competitive conditions, and stable environments—none of which characterize critical mineral markets. The monopsony power of China, the strategic manipulation of markets by state actors, and the potential for catastrophic disruptions all violate the conditions under which market efficiency claims are valid.

The second objection concerns allies and international order. Resource nationalism, critics argue, will alienate friendly nations, undermine the rules-based international order, and play into the hands of authoritarian powers who advocate for a multipolar world. This objection conflates American interests with the interests of particular international arrangements. The rules-based order has served American interests in many ways, but it should not be preserved at the cost of sacrificing vital interests. Moreover, the current international order already permits resource nationalism; nations like China and Russia have practiced it extensively without being ostracized. The United States should not unilaterally disarm in a world where others wield resource weapons.

The third objection concerns feasibility. The United States cannot quickly develop domestic capacity for critical minerals that have been offshored for decades, and restrictions on imports will simply create shortages without stimulating domestic production. This objection underestimates American technological and industrial capabilities while overestimating the difficulty of the task. The United States has abundant mineral resources, world-class mining and processing companies, and the financial capital necessary for large-scale investment. What has been lacking is policy support and market certainty. With strong policy signals, domestic capacity could be developed far more rapidly than critics suggest.

The fourth objection, perhaps the most serious, concerns the distribution of costs and benefits. Resource nationalism will raise prices for consumers and impose costs on industries that depend on cheap inputs. These costs will fall disproportionately on lower-income households and on regions that have benefited from export-oriented resource extraction. These distributional concerns are legitimate and should be addressed through policy design, but they do not undermine the fundamental case for resource security. The costs of dependency—including potential military vulnerability, supply disruptions, and price volatility—fall on everyone, while the benefits of resource security accrue disproportionately to those who depend most on reliable access. A well-designed resource nationalism policy would include measures to protect vulnerable consumers and communities while building the foundations for long-term security.

A Framework for American Resource Nationalism

Moving from principles to practice requires a comprehensive framework that identifies priorities, allocates responsibilities, and establishes mechanisms for implementation. The first element is assessment: a thorough, bipartisan evaluation of American resource vulnerabilities that identifies which dependencies create the most serious risks and which resources warrant the most urgent attention. This assessment should consider both current dependencies and projected future needs, particularly for minerals required in clean energy technologies and defense systems.

The second element is strategic reserves. The United States should build substantial reserves of critical minerals, managed apolitically and sized to buffer against significant disruptions. These reserves should include both processed materials and raw ores to ensure processing capacity as well. Energy reserves should be expanded and protected from political manipulation, with clear trigger mechanisms for release during supply emergencies. Water storage and conservation measures should be integrated into regional planning frameworks, particularly in water-stressed areas.

The third element is domestic capacity development. The federal government should provide support for mining, processing, and recycling of critical minerals, using a combination of investment incentives, regulatory streamlining for environmentally responsible projects, and procurement policies that guarantee markets for domestic producers. This support should be targeted at the most vulnerable supply chains and should include requirements for environmental standards, community benefit agreements, and worker protections that distinguish American production from the exploitative practices common in foreign extractive industries.

The fourth element is export management. The United States should establish mechanisms to restrict exports of critical resources when domestic needs warrant, using thresholds that ensure adequate supplies for domestic industry while allowing exports of surplus production. These restrictions should be calibrated to specific materials and adjusted as domestic capacity develops. They should be implemented through transparent processes with clear criteria to prevent arbitrary application.

The fifth element is international coordination. Resource nationalism need not mean going it alone. The United States should work with allies to diversify supply chains, share intelligence about resource vulnerabilities, and coordinate policies to prevent adversaries from playing divide-and-rule strategies. The minerals partnership launched with ally nations represents a promising model that should be expanded and deepened.

Conclusion

The case for American resource nationalism rests not on isolationism or autarky but on the most basic responsibilities of sovereign government: ensuring the security and prosperity of its people. The dependencies that have accumulated over decades of globalism represent strategic vulnerabilities that could be exploited by adversaries or amplified by disruptions beyond anyone's control. The United States has the resources, the technology, and the industrial capacity to reduce these vulnerabilities significantly. What has been lacking is the political will to prioritize long-term security over short-term convenience.

The Case for Protectionist Resource Nationalism in the United States

Resource nationalism represents a policy framework whereby governments assert substantial control over the extraction, processing, and distribution of natural resources within their territories, often through export restrictions, domestic processing requirements, or state-owned enterprise involvement. While free-trade advocates typically decry such measures as economically inefficient and potentially counterproductive, proponents advance several interconnected arguments suggesting that strategic resource protection can serve vital national interests. Understanding these arguments provides essential context for ongoing debates about trade policy, supply chain resilience, and national security in an era of intensifying geopolitical competition.

Ensuring Domestic Supply Security During Global Disruptions

The most immediate practical argument for export restrictions on critical resources concerns ensuring domestic availability during periods of international turmoil. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck in 2020, numerous countries experienced severe shortages of medical supplies, semiconductors, and other essential goods that they had relied on global supply chains to provide. Nations that had outsourced their manufacturing capacity found themselves at the mercy of foreign suppliers who, quite understandably, prioritized their own citizens during the crisis.

Proponents of resource nationalism argue that similar vulnerabilities exist with respect to natural resources. Consider the case of rare earth elements, which are essential for manufacturing smartphones, electric vehicles, defense systems, and countless other technologies. China currently controls approximately 60 percent of global rare earth mining and an even larger share of processing capacity. Should tensions between the United States and China escalate to the point of trade disruption, American manufacturers could find themselves unable to obtain materials necessary for both civilian economy and military readiness. By restricting exports of domestically mined resources and requiring strategic stockpiles, the argument runs, the United States can insulate itself from such supply disruptions.

The logic extends beyond wartime scenarios to encompass other forms of global disruption. Natural disasters, pandemics, shipping container shortages, port closures, and even diplomatic disputes can all interrupt the smooth functioning of global commodity markets. A nation that has ensured domestic control over its resource base possesses greater autonomy in navigating these challenges, regardless of their origin.

Stabilizing Domestic Industries Against Price Volatility

Global commodity markets are notorious for their dramatic price fluctuations, which can devastate domestic industries that depend on steady input costs. Oil prices collapsed in 2014-2016, devastated American shale producers, and then spiked in 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Lithium prices increased by over 400 percent between 2020 and 2022 before declining substantially in 2023. Such volatility creates severe planning challenges for manufacturers and can force painful workforce decisions.

Resource nationalism advocates contend that export restrictions can serve as a stabilizing mechanism by separating domestic prices from international market swings. When a country restricts exports of a commodity, domestic supply increases relative to global supply, which tends to dampen price increases during periods of international shortage. Conversely, during periods of global oversupply, domestic producers still have access to their home market even as international prices collapse. This buffering effect can allow domestic industries to maintain more stable employment and investment patterns.

The steel and aluminum industries have historically made precisely this argument in favor of trade protections. They contend that cyclical global overcapacity, particularly from countries like China, creates unfair competition that destabilizes American producers and threatens national manufacturing capability. By restricting imports or limiting exports of competing inputs, the reasoning goes, the government can help smooth out these boom-and-bust cycles that otherwise plague resource-dependent industries.

Preserving Strategic Resources for Future Generations

A more long-term argument for resource nationalism concerns the finite nature of many mineral resources and the strategic importance of ensuring adequate reserves for future decades. Some estimates suggest that known reserves of certain critical minerals may be depleted within decades at current extraction rates. The transition to clean energy technologies, for instance, requires massive increases in lithium, cobalt, nickel, and graphite production—minerals whose geographic distribution is highly concentrated and whose extraction often involves significant environmental costs.

From this perspective, the argument for export restrictions becomes analogous to the reasoning behind petroleum strategic petroleum reserves. Just as the United States maintains underground caverns filled with emergency oil supplies, proponents argue that the nation should maintain "resource sovereignty" over its most strategically important mineral deposits. Exporting these materials now at depressed prices, while depleting domestic reserves, may prove shortsighted when future generations face even greater resource constraints.

This argument carries particular weight for minerals that lack viable substitutes and that will be essential for emerging technologies. The International Energy Agency has projected that achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 will require a four-fold increase in critical mineral production. Nations that have exported their mineral wealth during the extraction boom may find themselves importing these same materials at vastly higher prices and under less favorable terms once their deposits are exhausted.

Protecting Vulnerable Supply Chains from Foreign Control

Contemporary supply chain vulnerabilities extend beyond simple availability concerns to encompass the geographic concentration of processing capacity. For many resources, the raw material may be mined in one country, refined in a second, manufactured into components in a third, and assembled into final products in a fourth. This fragmentation creates numerous potential points of failure, any of which can disrupt the entire chain.

China's dominance in critical mineral processing represents a particularly salient concern. While the United States and Australia produce significant quantities of lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements, the vast majority of these materials are shipped to China for refining before reaching downstream manufacturers. This processing concentration means that even resources mined in allied nations remain vulnerable to Chinese policy decisions. Proponents of resource nationalism argue that the United States should develop domestic and allied processing capacity rather than depending on potential adversaries for this essential transformation step.

Export restrictions can theoretically encourage investment in downstream processing by guaranteeing domestic manufacturers access to raw materials. If a company knows that it can rely on stable domestic supply of lithium ore or rare earth concentrate, it becomes more plausible to invest in the refining and manufacturing facilities that would otherwise seem risky given global competition. In this interpretation, export restrictions serve not as an end in themselves but as a policy tool for building more complete national or allied supply chains.

Strengthening National Security and Defense Readiness

Perhaps the most consequential argument for resource nationalism concerns military readiness and defense capability. Modern weapon systems depend on an astonishing array of specialized materials—rare earth magnets in precision-guided munitions, lithium batteries in electric vehicles and aircraft, titanium in jet engines, and countless other inputs whose supply must be assured during wartime conditions.

The Department of Defense has increasingly recognized supply chain vulnerabilities as a national security concern. Recent legislation has directed the Pentagon to assess dependencies on foreign suppliers and to develop strategies for ensuring access to critical minerals. General Motors, Lockheed Martin, and other defense contractors have all highlighted the risks associated with concentrated global supply chains for essential materials.

From this perspective, resource nationalism represents a straightforward matter of military self-reliance. Just as the United States maintains domestic capacity for producing weapons systems rather than depending on foreign suppliers, it should ensure domestic access to the raw materials that those systems require. During major conflicts, enemy powers would certainly target supply lines and foreign suppliers, making domestic resource control a strategic imperative rather than an economic preference.

Maintaining Economic Sovereignty and Bargaining Power

Beyond the specific concerns of supply security and price stability, some advocates frame resource nationalism in broader terms of economic sovereignty. The argument holds that a nation that depends on foreign suppliers for essential inputs sacrifices a degree of autonomy in its foreign policy decisions. Countries that rely heavily on Russian energy, for instance, have found their ability to respond to Russian aggression constrained by concerns about energy security.

Resource nationalism advocates argue that maintaining domestic control over natural resources preserves diplomatic flexibility. A nation that can meet its own needs for critical materials faces fewer constraints in pursuing its strategic interests, regardless of the preferences of resource-exporting nations. This argument carries particular weight in the context of great power competition, where the ability to impose costs on adversaries without suffering reciprocal harm represents a significant strategic advantage.

Furthermore, control over resource supplies can enhance bargaining power in international negotiations. Nations that dominate critical mineral supply chains, like China's dominance in rare earth processing, can use this control as leverage in diplomatic disputes. The United States, according to this argument, should develop similar capabilities not to threaten others but to ensure that it cannot be coerced through resource dependencies.

Environmental and Labor Standard Considerations

An additional argument for resource nationalism concerns the environmental and labor implications of globalized extraction industries. Mining and resource processing can generate significant environmental impacts, including water pollution, habitat destruction, and greenhouse gas emissions. Labor conditions in some resource-producing countries fall well below standards that would be acceptable in the United States or other developed nations.

Proponents of resource nationalism argue that restricting exports of raw materials encourages domestic processing, which brings extraction operations under regulatory frameworks that environmental and labor advocates consider superior. A mine that ships its output overseas for processing may face fewer constraints on its environmental practices than one that must meet American standards before its materials can be sold. By requiring domestic processing, the government can ensure that resource extraction occurs under conditions that reflect domestic values regarding environmental protection and worker safety.

This argument connects resource nationalism to broader debates about globalization and its discontents. Critics of contemporary trade arrangements contend that global competition has created a "race to the bottom" in which countries compete to offer the most permissive regulatory environments rather than the highest standards. Resource nationalism, in this interpretation, represents an attempt to break from this dynamic by ensuring that at least some economic activity occurs within regulatory frameworks that value environmental and labor protections.

Criticisms and Limitations of Resource Nationalism

While these arguments for resource nationalism possess considerable merit, they must be weighed against substantial criticisms that economists and free-trade advocates have advanced. Export restrictions may provoke retaliatory measures from trading partners, potentially disrupting other economically important supply chains. They can also reduce incentives for domestic producers by limiting their access to potentially lucrative export markets, potentially slowing rather than accelerating the development of strategic industries.

Moreover, resource nationalism may prove ineffective if other nations possess sufficient supply to meet global demand without American exports. Restrictions on American rare earth exports, for instance, would primarily affect the distribution of a limited supply rather than ensuring American access to materials that remain controlled by foreign producers. The most effective approaches to supply chain resilience may involve building domestic processing capacity and developing recycled and alternative materials rather than simply restricting exports of raw materials.

Conclusion

The arguments for protectionist resource nationalism rest on legitimate concerns about supply security, economic stability, national defense, and strategic autonomy. In an era of intensifying geopolitical competition and increasing recognition of supply chain vulnerabilities, these considerations deserve serious policy attention. However, the implementation of resource nationalism policies requires careful calibration to avoid the economic inefficiencies and potential retaliation that have historically undermined protectionist approaches. The most robust strategy likely combines targeted restrictions on truly critical materials with broader investments in domestic processing capacity, allied supply chain development, recycling technologies, and materials substitution research. Resource nationalism, properly understood, represents not a return to autarky but rather a strategic insurance policy against the vulnerabilities that extreme globalized dependency can create.

I am proposing that we restrict exports of critical materials, rebuild our strategic reserves, and ensure that American resources serve American interests first.

This is not radical. This is not unprecedented. This is not even unusual. Nations throughout history, including our own, have recognized that certain resources require special protection. We do not allow the export of classified military technology. We restrict the sale of certain advanced weapons systems. We maintain strategic petroleum reserves that have been tapped during crises. The principle I am advancing is simply an extension of this established logic to cover the full range of critical resources upon which our economic and national security depends.

The economic case is compelling. When we export critical resources in raw or minimally processed form, we export jobs along with the materials. A ton of rare earth ore shipped overseas creates no American jobs beyond the mining operation itself. That same ton, processed into rare earth oxides, then into metals, then into magnets or catalysts, creates dozens of high-skilled American jobs at each stage of processing. By exporting unprocessed resources, we have systematically deindustrialized the downstream sectors that would create middle-class prosperity in communities that have been devastated by the offshoring of manufacturing. Resource nationalism means processing, manufacturing, and adding value on American soil, employing American workers, and strengthening American communities.

The national security case is overwhelming. Every major strategic assessment conducted by our government has identified critical material dependencies as vulnerabilities. The Pentagon has repeatedly warned that our defense supply chains are fragile. Our intelligence agencies have documented efforts by adversaries to control global supply chains as a means of creating leverage over the United States. The COVID-19 pandemic revealed the fragility of pharmaceutical supply chains dependent on foreign manufacturing. We must reduce our dependence on foreign sources to the greatest extent possible, and we must eliminate our dependence on adversarial sources entirely.

When we export raw materials for processing in nations with weaker environmental standards, we export pollution along with the resources. If we want to help developing nations, we should help them build their own industries, not perpetuate a system that keeps them in a state of dependent extraction.

The third objection will be that resource nationalism will raise costs for American consumers and businesses. To this I offer a simple response: the cost of dependence is higher than the cost of independence. When supply chains are disrupted, prices spike and shortages emerge. When adversaries control essential materials, they can impose political costs that far exceed any price increase from domestic production. The question is not whether we will pay for security but whether we will pay now, through investment in domestic capacity, or pay later, through vulnerability and coercion. The former is the path of strength. The latter is the path of weakness.

The fourth objection will be that such policies are protectionist and contrary to American values of free enterprise and open markets. I reject the false dichotomy between free enterprise and strategic resource management. American businesses have thrived when they compete on a level playing field with domestic competitors. They have suffered when supply chains are disrupted by events beyond their control. Resource nationalism does not mean abandoning market economics; it means ensuring that markets operate on a foundation of security and resilience. The Moment for Decision

Fellow Americans, we stand at a moment of decision. The forces that have shaped the global economy for the past three decades are in flux. The pandemic revealed vulnerabilities. The competition with strategic rivals has intensified. Climate change demands that we rebuild our energy and industrial systems. In each of these circumstances, the resources upon which we depend will be critical. The question is whether we will control those resources or whether we will remain dependent on supply chains we cannot influence.

I am not proposing that we turn inward, that we abandon our global engagements, or that we retreat from the world. I am proposing that we build from a position of strength, that we ensure our prosperity cannot be disrupted by events beyond our borders, that we create jobs and industries here at home rather than abroad. I am proposing that we learn from the strategies our competitors have pursued and pursue them ourselves—with the creativity, the technology, and the entrepreneurial spirit that have always made America great.

A Call to Action

I ask you to imagine the America we can build. An America where the resources beneath our feet fuel a renaissance of manufacturing. An America where the innovations born in our laboratories are produced in our factories. An America where the workers of Appalachia, the Mountain West, the Upper Midwest, and every resource-rich region of this country find dignity and prosperity in jobs that cannot be offshored. An America that cannot be coerced, that cannot be blackmailed, that cannot be brought to its knees by supply chain disruptions or economic warfare.

That America is within our reach. It lies not in some utopian fantasy but in the practical application of our abundant resources, our technological ingenuity, and our national will. It requires only that we recognize what is at stake, that we reject the failed doctrines of the past, and that we commit ourselves to the proposition that American resources belong to America and will serve American interests first.

The nations that will dominate the twenty-first century will be those that control the critical resources of the new economy—rare earths, lithium, cobalt, the materials that power clean energy and advanced technology. China has made this its national mission. Russia has used its resources as instruments of power. Other nations are positioning themselves for the resource competition ahead.

Where is America?

We have the resources. We have the technology. We have the workers. What we need is the will. We need to decide, as a nation, that our future is worth fighting for. We need to reject the false promise of globalized dependence in favor of the hard truth of strategic independence. We need to embrace resource nationalism not as an ideology but as a necessity.

The American people have always risen to meet the challenges of their time. We ended the Great Depression through industrial mobilization. We won the Second World War through production miracle. We reached the moon because we committed ourselves to a great national purpose. Now we face a different kind of challenge—not a war that will be won in a day but a competition that will be won or lost over decades. The weapons in this competition are not tanks and planes but mines and factories, processing facilities and manufacturing plants, research laboratories and skilled workers.

I believe we will rise to meet this challenge. I believe the American people understand what is at stake and are ready to demand that their government pursue their interests. I believe that when we look our children in the eye and tell them that we did everything we could to secure their future, we will be able to say with honesty that we fought for an America that controlled its own destiny.

The resources are there, beneath our feet, in our waters, across our vast and beautiful land. They are American resources. They belong to the American people. And it is time—past time—that we treated them that way.

This pattern will only intensify as climate change, population growth, and industrial competition accelerate resource scarcity worldwide. Fresh water represents perhaps our most critical resource—irreplaceable for agriculture, industry, and human survival. Yet America continues allowing multinational corporations to extract vast quantities of groundwater for export while domestic drought conditions intensify. The Colorado River basin crisis demonstrates how quickly water scarcity can threaten American communities.

A robust resource nationalism policy would establish water as a strategic national resource, prohibiting its export in bottled form or virtual form through water-intensive exported products. Priority allocation would ensure domestic agriculture, essential industries, and American communities receive guaranteed supplies before any consideration of external sales. This is not protectionism—it is prudent resource management that recognizes water's irreplaceable nature and national security implications.

Energy Independence: Beyond Economic Advantage

The United States has achieved remarkable progress toward energy independence, yet continues exporting massive quantities of natural gas, petroleum, and other energy resources while simultaneously remaining vulnerable to global market disruptions. True energy security requires treating domestic energy not merely as economic commodities but as strategic assets.

The national security implications are profound—energy independence means freedom from coercion and leverage in international relations.

Perhaps nowhere is resource nationalism more justified than regarding rare earth minerals and critical materials essential for advanced technology, renewable energy systems, and defense applications. America's dangerous dependence on foreign sources for these materials represents an existential vulnerability.

China currently dominates global rare earth production and processing, controlling approximately 85% of refined output. This monopoly position has already been weaponized through export restrictions during diplomatic disputes. America must respond by:

  1. Declaring critical minerals national security assets
  2. Building strategic stockpiles through aggressive domestic mining
  3. Prohibiting exports of domestically produced rare earths
  4. Developing comprehensive recycling programs to capture minerals from discarded technology
  5. Investing in processing infrastructure to eliminate foreign dependencies

The technological sovereignty of the United States depends entirely on secure access to these materials. No short-term economic benefit from their export can justify compromising this fundamental security requirement.

Economic Sovereignty Through Resource Control

Critics may claim resource nationalism contradicts free market principles and risks retaliation. However, this perspective fails to recognize how other nations already implement strategic resource policies. Free trade fundamentalism that treats critical resources as ordinary commodities represents a dangerous ideological blindness to strategic realities.

Resource nationalism would strengthen America's economic position through multiple mechanisms:

  1. Reduced input costs for domestic manufacturing, enhancing competitiveness
  2. Protection against supply disruptions that cripple production
  3. Leverage in international negotiations
  4. Incentives for domestic processing and value-added industries
  5. Job creation in resource extraction, processing, and manufacturing sectors

The economic benefits extend far beyond the immediate value of the resources themselves. By maintaining these resources domestically, America creates the foundation for an industrial renaissance based on secure supplies and predictable costs.

National Security Imperatives

Modern warfare and defense capabilities depend entirely on access to critical resources. Water sustains military operations and bases. Energy powers everything from tanks to aircraft carriers. Rare earth minerals make possible the advanced guidance systems, communications equipment, and weapons platforms that maintain American military superiority.

Allowing these resources to flow freely into potential adversaries' hands while leaving domestic supplies vulnerable to disruption represents a profound strategic error. Resource nationalism aligns perfectly with fundamental national security requirements by ensuring America maintains the material foundation for its defense industrial base.

Implementation Framework

Implementing resource nationalism requires a comprehensive policy approach:

  1. Establishing a National Critical Resource Agency with authority to monitor, regulate, and restrict exports
  2. Classifying specific resources as strategic national assets with export controls

Conclusion: Resource Nationalism as Strategic Necessity

As global competition for finite resources intensifies, America faces a fundamental choice: continue treating critical resources as mere commodities in an idealized free market, or recognize their strategic importance and implement policies that secure them for domestic needs.

The case for resource nationalism is compelling across economic, security, and sustainability dimensions. By protecting our water, energy, and critical minerals, the United States would not merely be acting in its short-term interests but securing the foundations of American prosperity, security, and sovereignty for generations to come.

In a world of increasing resource competition and strategic rivalry, securing America's resource foundation isn't protectionism—it's prudence. The time has come to recognize that resource nationalism represents not an ideological position but a strategic necessity for America's future.

The United States should adopt strict “resource nationalism” policies that prioritize domestic needs by securing access to critical natural resources—especially water, energy, and rare earth minerals—through aggressive stockpiling, tighter production controls, and severe restrictions or even bans on export when national security and economic resilience require it. In an era of intensifying great-power competition, climate volatility, and fragile global supply chains, treating critical resources as ordinary commodities is a strategic mistake. The country’s long-term prosperity and national defense depend on ensuring that essential inputs are available at home first, on predictable terms, and under U.S. control.

Critical resources are strategic assets, not normal products

Resource nationalism begins with a simple premise: some resources are too consequential to leave to market forces alone. Water is foundational for agriculture, public health, manufacturing, and power generation. Energy—both fuel and electricity—is the lifeblood of transportation, industry, and defense systems. Rare earth minerals and other critical minerals are essential for high-tech manufacturing, precision weapons, radars, batteries, grid infrastructure, and advanced communications. When these inputs face scarcity, price spikes, or geopolitical chokepoints, the consequences are not limited to consumer costs; they extend to national security readiness and industrial survival.

Export-driven policies that assume global markets will reliably supply allies and the U.S. can fail under real-world stress. When rival states impose their own controls, when conflict disrupts shipping routes, or when climate-driven droughts and disasters reduce supply, “free trade” does not automatically guarantee continuity. In those moments, domestic access becomes decisive—meaning the U.S. must treat critical resources as strategic assets and ensure they are available first for American needs.

National security demands supply priority at home

National security is not only about borders and weapons; it is also about sustainment. Modern defense systems depend on rare earth-based components, specialized alloys, magnets, semiconductors, and battery materials. If those inputs become scarce or expensive due to foreign policy decisions, production disruptions, or export restrictions by other countries, the U.S. risks delayed procurement, higher costs, and—most dangerously—capability gaps.

By heavily restricting exports and maintaining domestic stockpiles of critical minerals and energy resources, the U.S. reduces leverage that adversaries can exert by manipulating supply chains. Resource nationalism deprives potential enemies of the ability to starve U.S. industries while simultaneously benefitting from U.S. exports. This is not an abstract fear; it is a predictable outcome of interdependence under coercion. Countries that regard critical inputs as strategic will prioritize their own survival first. If the U.S. does not do the same, it essentially accepts asymmetrical risk.

Economic resilience requires insulating industry from global shocks

Even beyond defense, strict resource nationalism strengthens the domestic economy by stabilizing prices and preventing “export-first” policies from draining supply during shortages. In commodity markets, scarcity often triggers rapid price escalation. When that happens, industries that rely on inputs—manufacturers of vehicles, machinery, electronics, construction materials, and grid components—can be priced out of their own domestic production.

Export restrictions and bans can seem counterintuitive, but the alternative is often a cycle of dependency: exports strengthen foreign supply while domestic supply becomes tighter, which then increases costs and weakens U.S. industry. In strategic sectors—where scaling production takes years and substitutes may not exist—temporary shortages can become long-term industrial decline. Resource nationalism interrupts that cycle by reserving essential inputs for American firms, workers, and infrastructure projects.

Additionally, tight control over critical resources encourages domestic investment in extraction, processing, recycling, and refining. If companies believe they will be able to reliably secure materials for domestic use, they are more likely to invest in capacity rather than gamble on volatile international markets. Over time, this builds resilience rather than perpetuating dependence.

Hoarding is not irrational—it is strategic stockpiling

The term “hoarding” can sound selfish or wasteful, but policy design matters. Resource nationalism does not have to mean inefficient accumulation or neglect of conservation. It can be implemented as strategic stockpiling with clear thresholds, transparent triggers, and defined release schedules. For example:

  • Minerals and rare earths: Establish national reserves for materials with long lead times and limited substitutability (e.g., specific magnet and processing inputs).
  • Energy: Prioritize reserves for essential fuels and maintain strategic capacity for generation and grid reliability.
  • Water: Use strict allocation rules, drought contingency planning, and infrastructure improvements that prioritize municipal, industrial, and food security needs.

The principle is consistent: the U.S. should maintain “insurance” against shocks. Strategic reserves are normal for defense; it is rational to extend the same logic to essential inputs that determine whether the defense and industrial base can function during crises.

Water resource nationalism protects food security and public stability

Water is perhaps the clearest example of why export-oriented thinking is misguided. Water scarcity is increasingly shaped by climate change, prolonged drought, and over-extraction. When water availability tightens, the immediate harm is not theoretical—it shows up as crop losses, higher costs, strained municipal systems, and energy disruptions due to reduced cooling capacity and impacts on hydroelectric output.

A resource-nationalist approach to water means prioritizing domestic allocations, restricting export arrangements that could undermine long-term availability, and enforcing conservation and efficiency standards with security in mind. While large-scale “water exports” from the U.S. may not be the dominant concern today, the underlying issue is the same: critical inputs cannot be treated as globally tradable abstractions when domestic stability depends on reliable supply.

Rare earth minerals and critical processing capacity are bottlenecks

Rare earths and critical minerals are not just mined; they must be processed into usable compounds, separated, refined, and turned into components. That processing capacity is highly concentrated globally. If foreign processors control the bottleneck, the U.S. can face dependency even when domestic mining exists.

Export restrictions and tighter domestic prioritization can accelerate the build-out of downstream capacity: refining, separation, and manufacturing. If the U.S. commits to reserving critical materials for domestic industrial use—especially for defense and strategic technologies—then domestic processing industries have stronger incentives to scale. This can reduce vulnerability to supply chain manipulation and geopolitical coercion.

Further, severe export restrictions prevent a scenario where the U.S. mines or supplies critical feedstocks, only for other countries to convert them into finished high-value goods that the U.S. then must import at a premium. Resource nationalism shifts value capture back home: raw materials and processing capacity become a national capability rather than a foreign profit engine.

Addressing objections: “It will hurt allies” and “it will break trade norms”

Critics often argue that export bans would damage alliances, violate trade commitments, or trigger retaliatory measures. Those concerns deserve serious consideration—but they do not outweigh the strategic risks of dependency.

  1. Alliances require reliability, not favors. If the U.S. cannot maintain its own supply, it cannot meaningfully support allies in a crisis. Export restrictions can be structured with exceptions for allies under tightly controlled conditions, such as long-term contracts tied to U.S. reserve objectives, or priority allocations during emergencies.
  2. Trade norms are not sacred when survival is at stake. Global markets already feature strategic behavior—subsidies, sanctions, export controls, and industrial policy. The U.S. should not pretend it exists in a purely neutral marketplace. Resource nationalism is a rational response to how competitors behave.
  3. Retaliation is a cost, but dependency is a vulnerability. A policy that reduces U.S. exposure to coercion can be worth the risk of short-term friction. Vulnerability to manipulation can be far more damaging than the loss of some trading flexibility.

The real objective is not autarky. It is controlled sovereignty: ensuring critical needs are met domestically and preventing adversaries from using exports, prices, or logistics as levers against American interests.

The policy pathway: strict, targeted restrictions—not blanket chaos

Resource nationalism should be precise and disciplined. Strictness should focus on the most sensitive materials and the most dangerous risk periods, while still allowing limited trade that does not jeopardize domestic security.

A credible U.S. approach could include:

  • Export licensing for critical minerals and fuels with “priority to domestic use” as a statutory rule.
  • National stockpiles with legally defined thresholds and emergency activation triggers.
  • Domestic processing requirements for a portion of supply to ensure U.S. retains capability, not just raw material.
  • Drought and water security rules that prioritize essential uses and prevent contractual arrangements that undermine long-term availability.
  • Accelerated domestic permitting and investment incentives for extraction and refining—because restrictions without capacity building can create shortages.

This approach makes resource nationalism functional rather than symbolic. It secures inputs while also building the industrial base to use them effectively.

Conclusion: securing the nation requires securing its inputs

The United States should adopt strict resource nationalism policies because critical resources are foundational to both national defense and economic survival. In a world of supply chain fragility and geopolitical competition, export-oriented assumptions are not a strategy—they are a gamble. By hoarding essential materials through strategic stockpiles, reserving water and energy for domestic stability, and severely restricting or banning exports of rare earth minerals and other critical inputs when necessary, the U.S. can reduce vulnerability, stabilize key industries, and ensure that American needs come first.

Resource nationalism, done with discipline and targeted design, is not greed or isolationism. It is strategic insurance—an acknowledgment that sovereignty means controlling the inputs that make modern life, modern industry, and modern defense possible.

That is what resource nationalism means—American control over American destiny.

The world is not going to suddenly become safer. Supply chains are not going to magically become more stable. Rivalries are not going to disappear because we prefer a more optimistic narrative.

In a world fraught with uncertainty, the benefits of ensuring national security, economic sovereignty, and preparedness for environmental challenges make a compelling case for prioritizing the hoarding and judicious use of critical resources. Adopting such an approach would safeguard the American way of life and promote long-term prosperity within a framework of stability and control. Only by asserting control over its natural resources can America assure its preeminence in the global landscape of the future.
